findings.title: Google credential is overwritten with a zod SafeParse wrapper object, corrupting every refreshed credential
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the raw zod `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed data. The Google refresh path does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` and then `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, so the stored credential key becomes `{success: true, data: {access_token, refresh_token, ...}}` instead of the token object. Previously this was `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returned the data directly. On the next instantiation `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth` throws, so Google Calendar stops working for every user whose token has been refreshed once — and this happens regardless of whether credential sync is enabled. Use `.data` (or make the helper return the data).

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses nonsensical computed keys and strips everything except access_token
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the string `"[object Object]"` (Zod schemas don't override `toString`), so the object literal collapses to `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() }`. The comments say it should accept a numeric expiry and pass through other properties, but zod's `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, so when credential sync is enabled the parsed `data` contains only `access_token`. Consequences in sync mode: Zoom computes `key.expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined * 1000` → `NaN`, which then fails `zoomTokenSchema.parse` on the next call ("Zoom credential keys parsing error"); Office365 never gets a new `expires_in` so the token is treated as expired and refreshed on every request; Google loses `expiry_date`. Use `.passthrough()` / `.catchall()` or an explicit expiry field instead.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token is injected even when sync is disabled, overwriting the real Office365 refresh token
findings.body: After parsing, the helper unconditionally sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` whenever the response lacks one — including the normal (non-sync) path. Office365's `refreshTokenResponseSchema` declares `refresh_token` as optional; previously a missing key was simply absent and the spread `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` kept the stored refresh token. Now, if Microsoft omits `refresh_token` in a refresh response, the stored credential's real refresh token is replaced with the literal string `"refresh_token"` and persisted to the DB (office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 264–272), permanently breaking that calendar connection until the user reconnects. The placeholder should only be applied in the sync branch.

findings.title: Sync path returns a raw fetch Response regardless of the shape each caller expects
findings.body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the `fetch` `Response` object, but the callers were written around their original client's return type: Google reads `res?.data` (Gaxios response) → `undefined.access_token` TypeError; HubSpot treats the return value directly as a `HubspotToken`, so `expiresIn` is undefined (`expiryDate` becomes `NaN`) and a `Response` object is written to `credential.key`; Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin read `tokenInfo.data` (axios) → `undefined.error` TypeError. Only the callers that already consumed a `fetch` Response (Office365, Lark, Webex, Zoom, MS Teams) can work. The helper needs to normalize the sync response to the caller's expected shape (e.g. return parsed JSON and adapt each caller), otherwise the headline feature is broken for 4 of the 9 integrated apps.

findings.title: Credential sync request carries no authentication, exposing the self-hoster's token endpoint
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no secret header or signature, and the `response.ok` status is never checked. As shipped, any party who can reach the self-hoster's endpoint can request fresh third-party access tokens for any user id simply by guessing integer ids. The inbound webhook requires `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; the outbound call should at minimum send the same shared secret (e.g. in `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`) so the partner endpoint can authenticate Cal.com, and non-2xx responses should be surfaced as errors rather than passed to token parsing.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The new refresh block calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (imports are jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, http-error, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). This fails type-check and at runtime throws `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` inside `getClient`, which rejects `this.conn` and makes every Salesforce operation fail.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes on every instantiation, bypasses the sync helper, and builds the connection with the stale token
findings.body: `getClient` unconditionally calls Salesforce's token endpoint each time the service is constructed (no expiry check), even though jsforce was already configured with `refreshToken` and refreshes automatically. It also calls `fetch` directly instead of `refreshOAuthTokens`, so the credential-sync feature this PR introduces does not apply to Salesforce at all, and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` is only used for validation. After the refresh, the `jsforce.Connection` is still created with `credentialKey.access_token` (the old token) rather than `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the newly obtained token is written to the DB but never used for the request. Additionally `response.statusText !== "OK"` is a brittle success check (statusText can be empty), and the `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` branch is unreachable because the helper throws on failure.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's id as the third argument, whose contract is `userId: number | null` and which is sent to the partner endpoint as `calcomUserId`. In sync mode the self-hoster will look up (and return tokens for) the wrong user — potentially another user's Zoho Bigin credentials — and the team-credential guard (`userId` null) is defeated because a credential id is always truthy. `refreshAccessToken` receives `credentialKey`/`credentialId` only; the credential's `userId` needs to be threaded through.

findings.title: Zoom sync request uses directory name "zoomvideo" instead of app slug "zoom"
findings.body: The inbound webhook (`app-credential.ts`) resolves apps by slug and Zoom's slug/appId is `"zoom"` (see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts`). The outbound sync request sends `appSlug: "zoomvideo"`, so a partner that keys its implementation on the same slug it pushes credentials with will not recognize Zoom refresh requests. Every other call site uses the real slug (`google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`, ...).

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==` and no HTTP method restriction
findings.body: The secret check uses plain string inequality, which leaks timing information about how many leading bytes match; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers as other webhook handlers do. The handler also accepts any HTTP method (GET, DELETE...) and proceeds to write credentials, where it should reject anything but POST with 405.

findings.title: Body validation, decryption and JSON.parse failures are unhandled and surface as 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on malformed input, `symmetricDecrypt` throws on a wrong key/ciphertext, and `JSON.parse` throws on non-JSON plaintext. None are caught, so a partner sending a bad payload gets a generic Next.js 500 (and a stack trace in dev) instead of a 400 explaining the problem, making integration debugging harder. Wrap these in try/catch (or use `safeParse`) and return 400 with a message.

findings.title: No tests for the new shared OAuth helpers or webhook despite touching every OAuth refresh path
findings.body: The PR rewires the token-refresh path for Google, Office365, MS Teams, HubSpot, Lark, Webex, Zoom, Zoho CRM, Zoho Bigin and Salesforce through two new helpers and adds an unauthenticated-by-design webhook that writes credentials, yet adds no unit tests (the description acknowledges tests were not added). Even a small test of `parseRefreshTokenResponse` would have caught that it returns a SafeParse wrapper, that the computed-key schema strips fields, and that the `refresh_token` placeholder leaks into the non-sync path; a test of `refreshOAuthTokens` with the sync env set would have caught the Response-shape mismatch for Google/HubSpot/Zoho.
